source: My lady-in-waiting, Brit—Birgitta—comes from a high house. She'd make a suitable match, if a bit low in rank. But... I just don't know.
Low in rank, eh? Is that how it works?
Yes. In a perfect world, we would marry him to the daughter of a neighboring court to build strong ties, as I was at his age.
But all the eligible girls are tied up at the moment.
Whatever is to happen to my son, when it has been done, I am sure things will be made right in the end.
Everything will be all right, my lady. You must hope so.
I certainly do.
I must bid you adieu, my lady.
And I you.
Let us hope we walk again tomorrow.
Ah. Hello, Horatio.
I must admit, I hadn't thought I'd find you here.
The castle has a somber air.
Yes. Today is not a day for walking.
I believe it's safest if we part ways, lady.
Retire to somewhere quieter.
I believe you're right, Horatio.
Let us hope we can return to these summer strolls soon.
For now... farewell.
What ails you, Gerta?
I sense your unhappiness seeping through the floors of your chambers and into my kitchen.
My own son is against me. Is there anything worse in this world? What can a mother do?
Even though he is to be King, I still sense Hamlet has been against me. What can a mother do?
The same as I once did for a troublesome little Queen-in-the-making.
You mean... me?
Gerta, don't you remember? You were all scraped knees and dirty hair for years! Running with the hounds, clambering around the stables...
I told you then what I'll tell you now: children must be formed, through discipline, into adults.
Just as dough must be beaten nearly to its limit before it can rise, so too must Lord Hamlet be forced to leave his gloom.
I... I've tried, Irma, but I could never force my son from his grief before he's ready.
I believe he must find his own way out of this darkness.
(My lady merely needs a gentle push.)
(And I am the one to deliver it.)
With Claudius gone, can't we all simply take a reprieve from all this? From pressuring one another?
My son must find his own way. And now that he is to be King, I know he shall. I believe it in my truest heart.
Hmm. Perhaps. Perhaps bearing the mantle of his country will make his spine strong at last.
(My lady has shown Hamlet such gentleness.)
(I merely pray that he returns the deed when he sits the throne.)
Irma, lovely lovely lovely Irma!
My Prince.
Why did you invite me to this filthy kitchen, of all places?
We needed to speak, Hamlet. About you. You run amok in the castle, grieving like a great dramatist...
Meanwhile, my lady weeps, wishing her son would come back to her.
Hamlet is dead.
Only the one Hamlet, my lord. Please—treat your mother with respect—
No. I hear your request, but I feel no obligation to honor it.
Are all your spoons where they should be? I heard tell they were considering wandering around.
Hitting unsuspecting princes upon the rear? Wanting to discipline me like a child?
I imagine that would end very poorly.
My kitchen is full and well busy, Lord Hamlet. I have no time for idle chatter.
You're nothing but an old maid whispering in my mother's ear.
Until now, I have tolerated you merely... don't give me a reason to have you stabled like a cow.
My lady is distressed, Lord Hamlet. She wants to make amends. I have loved her since she was a child.
If you had any sense of obedience—
—Which I don't.
—Or any love deep in the fog of your madness!
Certainly no love, either.
You are truly hopeless, aren't you?
So they say. But at least I don't have one foot in the grave like you, old shrew.
Leave my kitchen. Now. At once. Out! Out!
My lady, he is incorrigible.
Your son. Do you know what he says to me? Me, Irma, the woman who tended him as a babe?
What now? I scarcely think I can stand to know.
He threatens me. In my own kitchen. He tells me I have one foot in the grave.
Oh, dear.
Something must be done, lady. If I learned anything with you as a girl, it's that children need firm rails to grow straight and tall.
A wall which gives when pushed is one which can be clambered over. You see?
I must try to speak with him again. I'll do so as soon as I can.
Mother, you have been a busy little bird... shrilling in everyone's ear about me.
Hamlet. As the Queen and as your mother, I-I-I insist you drop this act at once!
If not, I'll need to have the guards confine you to your room. Y-you're a nuisance to the whole castle in this mood.
S-so... Irma's right, you simply must listen to me! Act cheerful and polite, or stay in isolation. It's your choice!
You want me to put on an act?
Oh, but I have already. If you think my disgust is all but thinly-veiled now, you have only to wait.
You cheated me out of my inheritance by marrying that idiot Claudius as soon as you could remove Father's hat from the doorknob.
Then you have the gall to insist I act happy about it? You've made me look like a fool. The boy who would have been King, now forever a Prince.
I hate you. I loathe you.
Be silent at once!
No—you be silent, bitch.
I'll do whatever I please.
You will rob me of nothing more.
Hamlet, Hamlet, Hamlet.
You've gone too far, my boy. Too far for even the Lord's greatest forgiveness.
A son who would treat his mother so is utterly without any redeeming light.
My lady is blind with her pain. I must stanch this bleeding wound on her behalf.
And unlike Gerta, I am far less patient.
Please, Lord. Give me strength.
H-He battered her aside, Lord, as if she were nothing!
But she loves him more than anything in the world.
What do you want me to do, Lord? How shall I carry out Your justice?
Must I not strike evil when I see it?
For surely, the boy is evil. I see the devil within him.
Please, help me. Help me to kill him.
But I don't need you to guide my hand. This is the sort of dish I understand how to make.
I didn't come here to apologize.
Nor to grovel at your tomb.
But there's something... I never said to you.
I wish I'd died that night, the first time I tried to kill myself after Father's death.
Then you wouldn't have had to suffer like this.
You could have lived on, grieving the loss of one branch of your family tree all at once.
A-And you could have made a new life with him. With Claudius.
After Father's death, when I tried to end my life, when I frightened you--I've been thinking ever since then that I wish I'd succeeded.
But then, this past week, it was as though someone lit a candle on my life. There are new things to live for. I'm slowly finding my footing.
Everything's changed so quickly this summer. Sometimes nothing feels real. But I'm going to change, too, from today onward.
It won't be fast. And I still wake up each morning with a stone in my stomach. I don't think that will disappear.
But I no longer spend every day desiring my own death.
I only hope I can create a world that makes you smile upon me from Heaven.
I can only hope I'll see you soon.
No—I know I won't. Because you're among the angels. Or at the very least, waiting patiently for your turn.
Me... I'm going right to Hell.
I love you. I loved you, Mother. I'm sorry. So very, horribly sorry.
And I can't live carrying this feeling for long. It weighs me down, pulls me to the grave.
Lord, I'm a miserable idiot.
I want you to know that I never truly hated you.
And I never got to tell you in time. But someday...
Someday I'll see you again, and then you'll know that deep in my heart, I always wanted to be the son you needed me to be.
I'm sorry. I'll come to visit you as soon as I can. I swear it.
Why did you come?
To understand why.
Why did you kill them?
That poison was for you.
You, who caused my lady to suffer day and night and tear her hair!
You, who turned on her, insulted her, threatened her—you ungrateful, disgusting child!
All my lady ever did was try to love you with all of her soul.
But you are not worthy of that love.
So you took matters into your own hands.
So be it. Allow me to take them into mine.
More bloodshed, Hamlet? Was that the solution?
All that brings is more death.
Had I let her live, she would have found a way to kill me.
You know of Irma's past. Of her history. Poison isn't the only 'solution' she can procure, even behind bars.
She left me with no choice.
They're gone.
It still doesn't feel real.
Then again, nothing has lately. Throw two more deaths into the fog. What does it matter?
My lady. If he treats you cruelly tonight—
He won't.
But if he does. Will you not see to it that he is disciplined?
He needs a mother, Irma. Not a militant leader.
Very well. I shall have the servants set the table.
Dinner is served.
Irma, this is wonderful, as always, my dear.
Of course, love.
Yes, many thanks, Irma. You've made my wife a happier—and plumper—woman during these hard times.
Laertes! Such a wonderful surprise to see you dining with us. I thought we'd lost you.
Ah, I'm soon to Paris, my lady. This is merely a temporary stay.
Well, I'm certainly glad to have you with us a little longer. And I'm certain your father is, too.
Aren't you hungry?
My appetite fails me. Perhaps it's just a stench on the wind, blowing in from the graveyard.
Oh, Hamlet.
Enough. Sit up straight. Look at your mother when you speak to her.
Or what?
Or I'll have to teach you discipline at the tip of my blade.
You ought to have sent me away when you had the chance.
Please. You make a weak child of yourself, and an embarrassment to your father.
Were he here, he would look upon you with only shame. He was ten times the man you are.
Some of us have more class.
What did you say, you lute-brained fop?
Is that the best you've got?
No one asked you to stay here in Denmark. We thought you were leaving, and I, for one, was overjoyed.
You're joking, surely? Watching the bottom fall out of your entire life is far better than anything I could have seen in Paris.
No, I'm glad I stayed.
I'm leaving. My appetite fails me.
Not until this madness you express has subsided.
Then we will all be waiting a while for my behavior to become pleasant, I expect.
My food looks like it was pushed around by a pig's snout. It's insulting.
Oh, Hamlet. How can you be like that?
